summary.text:
The largest borrower we have read. Brent's capital financing requirement closed 2025/26 at £1,412.3m against £1,074.1m of external loans, and its own forecast takes the CFR to £1,827.9m by 2029/30 on £495.8m of new borrowing over six years. The authorised limit has been raised from £1,800m to £2,000m. The reporting is quarterly, detailed and compliant — every indicator is there, with limits and a confirmation that none was breached.

The line worth reading twice is headed, in the council's own words, Investments Funded by Borrowing: £287.5m, rising to £326.4m. Most of it is lending to Brent's own housing companies — i4B Holdings has £179.2m of loans and £43.9m of equity, First Wave Housing £33.4m — with a new £32m loan and £8m of equity going in during 2026/27, against an approved limit of £500m. The rest is schools, academies and the West London Waste Authority.

That is a legitimate model and Brent is explicit that it is not investing for yield: the paper states the council 'has not undertaken any activities to invest for a yield or have any commercial plans'. Lending to a wholly-owned housing company is a service investment, not a commercial one. But the paper also states the return on those service investments — 2.60% in 2025/26, forecast at 3.00% — and, elsewhere, total interest payable of £41.1m on £1,074.1m of external loans. Whether the return covers the cost of the borrowing behind it is not a question the report puts, and it is the one that matters on £287.5m.

Internal borrowing is the other outlier. Most councils' internal borrowing is shrinking as reserves run down. Brent's grows, from £276.5m to £337.2m next year and £449.9m by 2029/30 — while balance sheet resources are held at exactly £453.6m in every forecast year. A figure that does not move across six years is an assumption rather than a forecast, and it is the assumption the whole liability benchmark rests on.

Two things are genuinely reassuring. Affordability improves rather than worsens: financing costs fall from 9.0% of the net revenue stream to 6.6% by 2030/31, because the revenue stream grows from £431.4m to £611.6m faster than the £41.9m of financing costs. And the £59.5m of LOBO debt is being retired on a schedule — £39.5m next year, nil by 2030/31 — which is the opposite of most LOBO books we see.

One caution for anyone quoting the tables: the service-investment total prints as £32.5m in the 2027/28 column where the components sum to about £295m, and the financing-cost heading is dated 2067/27. Both are plainly typographical, but they are in the version members read.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your quarterly treasury reporting. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Scope first. We hold 67 PWLB loans for Brent at a balance of £861.3m, against £1,074.1m of external loans in your own reporting — the £59.5m of LOBOs and the rest of the market debt sit outside a PWLB file, so nothing below is a claim about your whole book.

Your reporting is among the more complete we read — every indicator present, limits alongside actuals, and an explicit confirmation that none was breached. That is not universal and it is worth saying.

The line we keep coming back to is the one you head Investments Funded by Borrowing: £287.5m, rising to £326.4m, most of it lending to your own housing companies — i4B Holdings at £179.2m of loans and £43.9m of equity, First Wave Housing at £33.4m — with a further £32m loan and £8m of equity going in during 2026/27 against a £500m approved limit. Brent is explicit that this is what it is, which is the right way to present it.

The reason it interests us is that the two sides now move independently. The borrowing side reprices with the PWLB curve; the lending side is fixed in agreements with the companies. Your CFR goes to £1,827.9m by 2029/30 on £495.8m of new borrowing over six years, and the authorised limit has already been raised from £1,800m to £2,000m. Every tranche of that £495.8m gets priced on the day it is drawn — ten-year certainty closed at 5.83% this afternoon on notice 314/26, twenty-year at 6.38%, fifty-year at 6.27% — while the return side was set when each facility was agreed. We have no view at all on the model; we only note that the spread between the two is a live number rather than a settled one, and it is not visible from either side alone.

Something specific from our own data that we think is genuinely useful here, because it runs both ways. Your PWLB book splits almost evenly on today's premature repayment curve: 29 loans, £449.1m of principal, sit about £83.5m below par, while 38 loans, £412.2m, sit about £20.9m above. That £20.9m of premium is one of the larger premium positions we hold — most councils' books are one-directional because they were written in one era, and yours plainly was not. Netted it is about £62.6m of discount, but the net figure hides the more interesting fact. Standard caveats and we mean them: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On the near end: 12.6% of debt, £133.8m, falls due inside twelve months against a 40% ceiling, and 50.3% runs beyond ten years with 10.8% beyond forty. That is a comfortable shape and it means the £495.8m is the story rather than the existing book. July's sector borrowing was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — worth knowing when your own plan needs £176.9m in 2026/27 alone. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four fit Brent. Lending to & financing council companies is written for exactly the i4B and First Wave position. Subsidy Control Act 2022 for treasury & lending and Expected credit losses under IFRS 9 (ECL) sit alongside it — the ECL one matters more since the 2024 MRP amendments tied credit losses to the MRP charge on capital loans made from May 2024. And Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, given a CFR heading for £1,827.9m. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
